query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The catalytic performance of transition‐metal catalysts is governed by in situ transient changes in surface oxidation states that dynamically modulate adsorbate binding energies, thereby altering activity, selectivity, and durability.
generation.material_initial_state: Transition-metal catalysts with mixed-metal surfaces in their initial, as-synthesized state (prior to reaction initiation) exhibiting a baseline distribution of oxidation states.
generation.intervention: Perform near-ambient-pressure spectroscopic measurements (XPS/XAS) under systematically varied reaction conditions (temperature, gas composition, and partial pressures) to induce and monitor transient changes in surface oxidation states.
generation.conditions: Standard catalytic operating conditions typical for transition-metal catalysts (moderate to high temperature, relevant chemical feed, and pressure ranges) during real-time reaction monitoring.
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic changes in the local oxidation state and electronic structure at active sites, as evidenced by shifts in binding energies and near-edge spectral features measured by in situ XPS/XAS.
generation.mechanism: Variations in reaction conditions induce transient oxidation state changes on the catalyst surface, which in turn alter adsorbate binding strengths. This modulation of binding energies directly affects the balance between adsorbate activation and desorption, thereby controlling catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Catalysts that display larger transient shifts toward higher oxidation states during reaction conditions will show enhanced activity and improved durability relative to a baseline catalyst with stable or minimal oxidation state changes, though these shifts might also affect selectivity in a predictable manner.
generation.baseline: Catalysts operated under identical conditions that have been pre-treated or modified to suppress transient oxidation state changes, thus maintaining a relatively constant surface state.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should apply under operando conditions for dynamic, mixed-metal catalysts; it may not hold for catalysts with inherently stable or passivated surfaces such as certain oxides with fixed stoichiometry.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the extent of transient oxidation state changes and the resulting catalytic metrics (activity, selectivity, durability) remains uncertain, and may vary with catalyst composition and reaction type.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of catalysts with the same bulk composition. One group will be pre-treated to restrict surface oxidation state changes, while the other remains untreated. Operate both groups under identical reaction conditions while simultaneously performing in situ near-ambient-pressure XPS/XAS to track transient oxidation state changes and measuring catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
measurements: Time-resolved XPS binding energy shifts and XAS near-edge features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant correlation is found between the magnitude of transient oxidation state changes (or their suppression) and any measurable differences in catalytic performance (activity, selectivity, or durability) relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this article, we found that HEA surface with spatially varying adsorption free energy of H* (ΔGH*) circumvents the Sabatier principle of HER. DFT calculations indicate that the ΔGH* on HEA catalysts follows a Gaussian distribution [X ~ N(μ, σ2), μ: expectation; σ: standard deviation] due to the gradient electron distribution and the diffusion of H* on HEA surface is fairly easy with the small barrier of 0.232 eV. Some sites with strong adsorption (ΔGH* < μ − σ) are used for H* adsorption, while some sites with weak adsorption (ΔGH* > μ + σ) are used for H2 formation. It means that the catalytic activity for HER will be better if the μ is closer to 0 eV and the σ is larger, which is defined as an unusual Sabatier principle. The μ and σ values could be regulated by the composition, strain effects, and synthesis conditions of HEA catalysts. Guided by these theoretical findings, a PtFeCoNiCu catalyst with electron and composition gradients has been precisely fabricated, exhibiting excellent catalytic performance with an overpotential of 10.8 mV at −10 mA cm−2 and more than four times higher intrinsic activity over the state-of-the-art Pt/C. decision.trend: Starting with single-atom alloy investigations to break traditional scaling relations (PMC6203812), researchers pursued more complex multi-element mixes to achieve compositional tuning and robust catalyst performance (PMC7069714, PMC9260516). Subsequent efforts employed nanostructured or crystal-glass compositions (PMC9635819), high-entropy oxides (PMC10061923, PMC10517924), or rapid-synthesis high-entropy nanoparticles (PMC10288253) to optimize catalytic activity and stability. Recent work has highlighted the role of unique energetic landscapes (PMC10774414), multi-state coverage competition (PMC10949192), and strain-sensitive active sites in explaining improved performance, yet the direct, overarching mechanistic “key parameter” that unifies these synergy effects remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: Despite growing evidence that compositional complexity and local electronic structure can break conventional activity–selectivity constraints, it is still unclear which specific factor—surface electronic states, bonding configurations, or dynamic site restructuring—ultimately governs catalytic behavior across diverse transition-metal catalysts.
decision.lever: Perform near-ambient-pressure spectroscopy (e.g., XPS/XAS) under systematically varied reaction conditions (temperature, gas composition, partial pressures) to measure transient surface states and correlate these directly with measured activity, selectivity, and deactivation trends in real time.
decision.why: This approach builds on the emerging emphasis on synergy and dynamic site evolution in multi-element catalysts. By tracking surface chemical states during reaction, one can pinpoint how real-time changes in local composition, oxidation state, and adsorbate coverage dictate performance, providing a direct test of the proposed mechanistic factor that controls catalytic activity and durability.
